metadata.note: The Pacific Electric Railway was the largest electric interurban system ever built: at its 1920s peak more than 1,000 route miles of 'Red Car' lines radiated from Los Angeles to Long Beach, San Pedro, Santa Monica, Pasadena, Glendale, the San Fernando Valley, Santa Ana, Newport Beach, Pomona, San Bernardino, Riverside and Redlands. Henry Huntington incorporated the first Pacific Electric on 14 November 1901 and opened the Long Beach line on 4 July 1902; the Great Merger of 1 September 1911 folded Huntington's PE together with the Los Angeles Pacific, the Los Angeles Inter-Urban, the Los Angeles and Redondo, San Bernardino Valley Traction, San Bernardino Interurban, Redlands Central and Riverside and Arlington into one Pacific Electric Railway under Southern Pacific control. Passenger mileage was cut back steadily from the 1920s; PE sold its passenger business to Metropolitan Coach Lines on 1 October 1953, keeping only the Santa Monica Air Line, which it closed three weeks later. The publicly owned Los Angeles Metropolitan Transit Authority took over on 3 March 1958 and the last Red Car ran on the Long Beach line on 9 April 1961.
metadata.colour_note: Seven companies appear in this layer and each was given one colour, checked programmatically against every colour already in data/ so that none of them collides with an existing one. Pacific Electric Railway #FF3B30 (deliberately clear of Southern Pacific's #C1272D); Metropolitan Coach Lines #9A348E; Los Angeles Metropolitan Transit Authority #00A86B; Los Angeles Pacific Railroad #FF9F1C; Los Angeles Inter-Urban Railway #18A0FB; San Bernardino Valley Traction Company #046307; Riverside and Arlington Railway #D6A2E8. LAMTA (1958-1964) is treated as a separate company from the modern Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority (#0072BC in data/la_metro_rail.geojson), which was created in 1993 out of different predecessors.
metadata.ownership_note: Rule 4 splits are made wherever the company that ran the trains actually changed: Los Angeles Inter-Urban Railway or Los Angeles Pacific Railroad before PE leased them in 1908/1911, then Pacific Electric, then Metropolitan Coach Lines (sale completed 1 October 1953), then LAMTA (3 March 1958). Each is a separate feature carrying identical geometry. The Great Merger of 1911 is deliberately NOT a split point for lines PE already ran: Southern Pacific acquired control of the stock, but the operating company kept the Pacific Electric name, livery and timetables until 1953, so no new operator's name appears in a segment note at 1911. That change is recorded as a segment boundary and in the notes instead.

not_yet_sourced: No Pacific Electric timetable was read for any line in this layer. Every headway_min is an estimate and is flagged as such in its own segment note; the only avg_speed_kmh with a real source behind it is the Santa Ana Line's, from Wikipedia's '75 minutes between termini' at the 1911 merger.

No end-to-end running time is published anywhere reachable for the Long Beach Line or the San Pedro via Dominguez Line. The May 1956 Metropolitan Coach Lines Long Beach-San Pedro public timetable (https://wx4.org/to/foam/maps/2Wx4/001/1956-05-18MCL_LongBeach-SanPedroPTT.pdf) would settle both, but it is a three-page image scan with no text layer.

The Watts Line's start year is contested three ways: ERHA 'probably 1904', Wikipedia's infobox 'c. 1906', and April 1907 for the separation of local service at Slauson Junction. 1907 is drawn because it is the only one with a stated mechanism.
The Watts Line's end year is contested: 2 November 1959 (the Wikipedia article, which names the bus substitution) against 1961-04-09 (Wikipedia's List of Pacific Electric lines). 1959 is drawn.
The Great Merger date is given as 1 September 1911 by most sources and 1 November 1911 by ERHA's Santa Ana page. Only the year matters at this map's resolution, but the conflict is real.
The Bellflower Line's last day is 24 May 1958 in Wikipedia's article body and 25 May 1958 in ERHA and the line list.

The 1.4 mi downtown Los Angeles approach shared by the Long Beach, Watts, Santa Ana and San Pedro features is hand-approximated. ERHA describes the real route as out east on Olympic Boulevard (E. 9th St) to Hooper Street and north on San Pedro Street to the 6th and Main elevated, but none of it survives and it has not been checked against a PE track map.

Whether the Long Beach Line's own terminal loop in Downtown Long Beach (Ocean Boulevard and Pacific Avenue, Morgan Yard) differed from the modern Metro A Line loop has not been checked; the milepost comparison suggests it did, by about a mile.

Lines not yet in this layer at all: the Hollywood Line and the West Hollywood / Beverly Hills services through the Hollywood Subway, the Whittier and Yorba Linda lines, the San Fernando branch of the Valley lines (North Sherman Way to San Fernando, 27.47 mi from the Subway Terminal, cut 1 June 1938), the Soldiers Home branch off the Air Line at Home Junction, the Redondo Beach, El Segundo and Torrance lines, the Ocean Park and Venice extensions beyond Santa Monica on the Sawtelle line, and the Catalina Dock line.

The Venice Short Line and the Sawtelle line are drawn only from their 1908 standard-gauging under the Los Angeles Pacific, not from the narrow-gauge electric service the Pasadena and Pacific Railway ran over the same streets from 1896-97. That is a real omission of twelve years of electric passenger service, left out because it was a different company on a different gauge and no colour or route detail was researched for it - not because Rule 5 excludes it.
The Sawtelle line's traced length is 15.9 mi against a documented 17.12, a 7% shortfall that has not been run down.

The Pasadena Short Line is drawn only from PE's 1902 standard-gauge through service, not from the 6 May 1895 electrification of the Fair Oaks horsecar corridor by the narrow-gauge Pasadena and Los Angeles Electric Railway. Those 1895-1902 years belong to a different company running a different gauge over only part of the drawn route, and are left out rather than asserted.

The Redlands geometry is 8.3 mi against a documented 9.16 and the Riverside-Rialto geometry is a six-vertex hand approximation: both corridors are gone and neither is mapped in OSM, so their shapes should not be trusted at street level even though their endpoints and lengths are about right.

Sierra Madre's opening is given as 1 January 1906 (Wikipedia) for through service; ERHA dates the first double-track section 19 March 1904 and the extension 1906. The 1904-1906 partial service is not drawn, because where that first section ran has not been established.

ERHA says the 1906 Sierra Madre extension was built by the Los Angeles Inter-Urban. The Oak Knoll line, also LAIU-built in 1906, is split into an LAIU feature for 1906-1908; Sierra Madre is not, because no source says the LAIU rather than PE ran its trains. If one does, it needs the same Rule 4 split.

The Sierra Madre shuttle's end is 6 October 1950 (ERHA, with the last car at 5:43 pm) or 28 December 1950 (ERHA elsewhere, and Wikipedia) - probably a franchise run like Oak Knoll's, but not confirmed.

The North Fair Oaks carhouse terminal of both Pasadena lines is not drawn; the line stops at Holly Street. The carhouse's exact location was never sourced, and OHM's stop dates put the passenger terminal at Holly Street from 1941.
rule_notes: Rule 1: every segment ends at that line's last PASSENGER run. Pacific Electric freight over these corridors long outlived the Red Cars - Southern Pacific and later Union Pacific worked much of the Long Beach route into the 1980s, and the Santa Monica Air Line carried freight for decades after 1953 - and none of that is drawn.

Rule 5: the Santa Monica Air Line's corridor was a steam railroad from 1875, not an animal-worked one, but it is still drawn only from its 1908 electrification, and only over the part that was electrified then. No line in this layer is drawn over years of horse or mule haulage.

Rule 7: mode is 'interurban' (drawn dashed) throughout - these were electric railways built to link separate communities, including the Watts Line, which was PE's own local over an interurban trunk. The Los Angeles Railway 'Yellow Cars', the narrow-gauge local streetcar company, is a different operator and is not in this layer.

Rule 2: most of this layer is STREET-TRACED rather than rail-traced, because almost nothing of the Pacific Electric survives as railway in OpenStreetMap. Only three features have real right-of-way geometry from OpenStreetMap under them: the Santa Ana and Bellflower lines (the surviving West Santa Ana Branch, still tagged old_railway_operator='Pacific Electric Railway'), and the Claremont-to-Rialto half of the Upland-San Bernardino line (the Pacific Electric Trail, built on the grade). Everything else is either a modern light-rail alignment on the old right of way (Metro A and E Lines), a street centreline where PE ran in or beside the street, or a hand-drawn approximation. Every feature's geometry_quality says which of those it is, leg by leg, with mileages.

Rule 2 (continued): the Northern District features - the Pasadena Short Line, both Oak Knoll features, Los Angeles - Monrovia, Monrovia-Glendora, Sierra Madre and the Sierra Madre shuttle - are traced from OpenHistoricalMap route relations instead, drawn from historical aerial photographs and a 1981 Caltrans track inventory. Each geometry_quality names its relation id, and the traced lengths are all within 3% of ERHA's mileposts.

properties.speed_source: ESTIMATE, 20.37 route miles. No end-to-end running time for this line is published by either Wikipedia or ERHA, and the one primary source that would settle it - the May 1956 Metropolitan Coach Lines Long Beach-San Pedro public timetable - is an un-OCRed image scan. ERHA's system table caps PE average speeds at 30.6 mph (San Bernardino) and 30.1 mph (Newport-Balboa), so a Long Beach average in the low-to-mid 20s mph is the defensible figure; 40 km/h is about 25 mph.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced 20.2 mi against a documented 20.37 mi (ERHA milepost table: LA 0.00, Slauson Jct 4.27, Watts 7.45, Dominguez Jct 13.31, North Long Beach 17.52, Long Beach 20.37). WRONG-ERA GEOMETRY: the 18.3 mi from Long Beach Avenue at Washington south to 1st Street in Downtown Long Beach is drawn on the MODERN Metro A Line light-rail alignment (OSM route relation 2351005), rebuilt in 1987-90 on the Pacific Electric right of way it replaced. It follows the PE corridor closely - Long Beach Avenue, Watts, Willowbrook Avenue, Compton, Dominguez, the Los Angeles River crossing, Willow Street and Long Beach Boulevard - but it is a 1990 survey, not a 1902 one, and it does not reach PE's own Long Beach terminal at Ocean Avenue and Pacific Avenue. Cross-checking against the ERHA mileposts, the drawn line reaches Willow Street about 1.1 mi later than PE's MP 17.52, which is the size of the alignment difference at the Long Beach end. The remaining 2.0 mi into downtown Los Angeles is APPROXIMATED: 0.6 mi on Long Beach Avenue itself (OSM street geometry - PE ran on private right of way beside it) and 1.4 mi from 26th Street to the Pacific Electric Building at 6th and Main, hand-drawn, standing in for PE's real route out east on Olympic Boulevard (E. 9th St) and north on San Pedro Street to the downtown elevated, none of which survives or is mapped.

segments.note: Henry Huntington's original Pacific Electric Railway (incorporated 14 November 1901) opened this line on 4 July 1902 - the first long interurban of the system and the route the whole Red Car network grew out of. Standard gauge from day one; the original Los Angeles terminal was at 9th and Main. A Long Beach newspaper digest records regular service beginning 5 July 1902 'with ten minute service during the day', which is where the headway comes from; it is a snapshot of the opening years, not a figure held constant to 1911.
sources: Segment-level: the 4 July 1902 opening (officials' car 3 July), the 1901 incorporation and the ten-minute daytime headway at opening are from the ERHA Long Beach Line pages; the 1902-1911 span reflects Huntington's 'Old PE' before the Great Merger.

segments.note: From the Great Merger of 1 September 1911 the line was worked by the consolidated Pacific Electric Railway, a Southern Pacific subsidiary. Trains kept the Pacific Electric name and livery throughout, so this feature is not split at 1911 (see the layer's ownership_note). PE's busiest interurban: four tracks from Amoco Junction south to Watts, private right of way almost throughout, one short single-track section on the Los Angeles River bridge, six curves and a maximum grade of 1%. Headway is an ESTIMATE - no PE timetable was consulted.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the 1 September 1911 Great Merger and Southern Pacific control are from the Pacific Electric overview and ERHA's Western District summary, and the four-track/single-track-bridge description is from the ERHA Long Beach page, but no timetable was checked for the headway or for service in any particular year of this segment. Sources also conflict on the merger date: 1 September 1911 (Wikipedia, ERHA Western summary) against 1 November 1911 (ERHA's Santa Ana page).

properties.line: Los Angeles Pacific: Santa Monica Air Line
properties.speed_source: ESTIMATE. 16.88 route miles. ERHA gives no average speed for the Air Line; 45 km/h (28 mph) is assumed from its limited-stop 'flyer' character on almost wholly private right of way, by analogy with PE's fastest lines (San Bernardino 30.6 mph, Newport-Balboa 30.1 mph in ERHA's system table). properties.geometry_quality: The western 5.72 mi only, Culver Junction to Santa Monica, drawn on the MODERN Metro E Line light-rail alignment (OSM route relation 6584633) rebuilt on the Air Line right of way in 2010-16 - see the full-route feature for how good that fit is. The line is cut at Culver Junction deliberately: only Sentous (MP 10.04) westward was electrified in 1908, and until the Amoco Junction-Culver Junction section was energised in 1912 electric cars left the Air Line at Culver Junction and ran to the Hill Street terminal over the Venice Short Line, which is not drawn in this layer.

segments.note: The corridor was built in 1875 as the steam Los Angeles and Independence Railroad (first train 17 October 1875) and sold to Southern Pacific in 1877; SP leased it to the Los Angeles Pacific Railroad in 1908, which electrified Sentous to the Long Wharf that year. Electric service to the Hill Street terminal began in July 1908, cars running east from Culver Junction over the Venice Short Line; a limited 'flyer' service was inaugurated on 26 May 1909. Only the portion drawn here was electrified before 1911-12. Headway is an ESTIMATE.

properties.line: Los Angeles Inter-Urban: San Pedro via Dominguez
properties.speed_source: ESTIMATE. 24.43 route miles. Neither ERHA nor Wikipedia publishes a headway or a running time for this line, and the May 1956 MCL Long Beach-San Pedro public timetable that would settle it is an un-OCRed image scan. 40 km/h (25 mph) is carried over from the Long Beach Line, whose trunk it shares.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced 23.8 mi against a documented 24.43 mi to the San Pedro passenger station (ERHA mileposts: Watts 7.38, Compton 10.91, Dominguez Jct 13.32, Flint Jct 19.11, Wilmington 20.13, San Pedro 24.43, Outer Harbor 25.39 - Wikipedia's infobox uses 25.39, which is the freight end, and its station table says 22.68). Two pieces. It is drawn about 110 m west of the OSM centreline of Alameda Street, which is where ERHA places PE's dual track (immediately west of Alameda, alongside the Southern Pacific branch), then hand-drawn southwest to the Wilmington station at Avalon Boulevard and B Street, across the West Basin and down into San Pedro. segments.note: From the Hill Street station south on Hill Street and west on Venice Boulevard to Vineyard Junction, where it turned northwest off the Venice Short Line on a grade separation over Pico, then on private way in the centre of San Vicente Boulevard across La Brea, Hauser, Fairfax, Wilshire and La Cienega to Sherman Junction, along the centre of Burton Way to Beverly Hills, and out Santa Monica Boulevard through Sawtelle and West Los Angeles into Santa Monica. Into Pacific Electric at the 1911 Great Merger. Limited trains were introduced in December 1927 and a morning limited added in October 1928; ridership peaked at 2,644,512 in 1929. The 1933 cuts took the base headway to 40 minutes, 30 at night and on Sundays, with a 60-minute Hill Street to Santa Monica running time, and that held substantially to the end. Service was virtually discontinued after 7 July 1940 - a single daily franchise car ran Vineyard to Beverly Hills after that - and the line was formally abandoned on 18 November 1940.
